facts.statement: The first remains of Mariliasuchus were collected in 1995 by the Brazilian paleontologist William Nava.
facts.quote: The first bone remains were found and collected in 1995 by Brazilian paleontologist William Nava

facts.statement: A second species, Mariliasuchus robustus, was named in 2007.
facts.quote: A second species, M. robustus, was named in 2007.

facts.statement: Fossils of Mariliasuchus have been discovered in close association with eggs, eggshells, and coprolites.
facts.quote: Several specimens of M. amarali have been found close to eggs, eggshells and coprolites to date

facts.statement: Fossils collected by William Nava were stored at the National Museum of Brazil but were partially destroyed in the 2018 fire.
facts.quote: The findings by William Nava could be found in the National Museum of Brazil, but they were partially destroyed in the 2018's National Museum of Brazil fire.

facts.statement: Mariliasuchus fossils come from the Adamantina Formation and date to the Late Cretaceous, possibly the Campanian or Maastrichtian stages.
facts.quote: They come from the upper part of the Adamantina Formation, indicating a Late Cretaceous (possibly Campanian/Maastrichtian) age.

facts.statement: Mariliasuchus lived between 83.6 and 66 million years ago during the Campanian to Maastrichtian stages.
facts.quote: Time range: Campanian to Maastrichtian (83.6 to 66 million years ago)

facts.statement: Mariliasuchus is an extinct genus of crocodyliforms.
facts.quote: taxon: Mariliasuchus

facts.statement: Mariliasuchus is classified as a notosuchian crocodyliform from the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Mariliasuchus ("Marilia crocodile") is an extinct genus of Late Cretaceous notosuchian crocodyliforms

facts.statement: Mariliasuchus belongs to the parent group Sphagesauria.
facts.quote: Parent group: Sphagesauria

facts.statement: Unlike modern crocodiles, Mariliasuchus lived primarily on land.
facts.quote: Mariliasuchus, unlike modern crocodylians, was an animal of terrestrial habits (though see below).

facts.statement: Mariliasuchus had nostrils located on the front of its skull, unlike the upward-facing nostrils of modern crocodiles.
facts.quote: Its nostrils were located on the front of the skull, unlike modern crocodiles, in which the nostrils face upwards

facts.statement: The eyes of Mariliasuchus faced laterally, whereas modern crocodile eyes face upwards.
facts.quote: Furthermore, the eyes in M. amarali are faced laterally (in modern crocodiles they face upwards).

facts.statement: Mariliasuchus possessed a highly modified dentition consisting of incisiform, caniform, and molariform teeth.
facts.quote: It had a very modified dentition, differentiated in incisiforms, caniforms and molariforms.

facts.statement: The front teeth of Mariliasuchus were directed horizontally instead of vertically.
facts.quote: Strangely, in particular, were the anterior-most teeth, which were directed horizontally rather than vertically.

facts.statement: Mariliasuchus had strong jaw muscles, suggesting significant mandibular activity.
facts.quote: It also had strong jaw muscles, indicating a good degree of mandibular activity.

facts.statement: The enamel structure of Mariliasuchus suggests it may have eaten plants to some extent.
facts.quote: The thickness and uneven distribution of the enamel of Mariliasuchus suggests it may have consumed plants to some degree.

facts.statement: Enamel microstructure indicates Mariliasuchus had an omnivorous diet that included feeding on hard objects.
facts.quote: The enamel microstructure of M. amarali further supports the notion that this animal had an omnivorous diet with a considerable degree of hard object feeding.

facts.statement: Researchers inferred that Mariliasuchus had a sprawling posture and possibly amphibian habits similar to modern crocodilians.
facts.quote: Nobre and Carvalho (2013) inferred that Mariliasuchus did not have an erect or semi-erect posture, but rather a sprawling posture and, possibly, had amphibian habits similar to those of living crocodilians.

facts.statement: It is debated whether variations in Mariliasuchus specimens represent ontogeny, sexual dimorphism, or a separate species.
facts.quote: There seems to be a significant degree of variation between specimens of M. amarali. Some of this is related to ontogenetic variation, but some may also suggest sexual dimorphism, or even that some of the specimens assigned to this species belong to a different animal.

facts.statement: Studies show that as Mariliasuchus grew, its skull became shorter, more resistant, and laterally compressed.
facts.quote: Ontogenetic studies done by Vasconcellos and Carvalho (2005) concluded that during its growth, the skull of M. amarali individuals becomes shorter and the skull more resistant, while being laterally compressed.

facts.statement: In adult Mariliasuchus, the eye socket arrangement is less circular than in juveniles.
facts.quote: In adulthood, the orbit has a less circular arrangement than in younger individuals.

facts.statement: The postcranial skeleton of Mariliasuchus mixes traits found in terrestrial Cretaceous crocodyliforms and aquatic eusuchians.
facts.quote: The postcranial skeleton of Mariliasuchus amarali displays a mixture of traits similar to those present in the skeleton of Cretaceous terrestrial crocodyliform Notosuchus and traits present in aquatic eusuchian crocodyliform, including living crocodilians.

facts.statement: The function of Mariliasuchus's horizontal front teeth is unclear, though comparisons with pigs suggest convergent dietary preferences.
facts.quote: The function of this strange arrangement is not yet clear, but comparisons have been made with the dentition of pigs, indicating that their dietary preferences may be convergent.

rejected.statement: Mariliasuchus was formally described in 1999 by the Brazilian paleontologists Ismar de Souza Carvalho and Reinaldo J. Bertini.
rejected.quote: Four years later, it was described as Mariliasuchus amarali, by Brazilian paleontologists Ismar de Souza Carvalho and Reinaldo J. Bertini.

rejected.statement: The species Mariliasuchus amarali was named to honor the Brazilian naturalist Sérgio Estanislaw do Amaral.
rejected.quote: The type species is M. amarali, which was named in honour of Sérgio Estanislaw do Amaral, Brazilian naturalist.
